content: Endogenous production of glutamine may not be sufficient to meet the metabolic demands of individuals suffering from severe gastrointestinal diseases. Experimental studies conducted on animal models with gastrointestinal disease have indicated that supplementing with glutamine could potentially improve clinical outcomes. This review specifically evaluates the evidence regarding the impact of glutamine supplementation in young infants diagnosed with severe gastrointestinal disease. The primary objective of this review was to determine whether supplemental glutamine affects mortality and morbidity rates in young infants with severe gastrointestinal disease. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering all records up to September 2014. Additionally, conference proceedings and reference lists from prior reviews were examined. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared glutamine supplementation to no supplementation in infants up to three months of age. These infants had to have severe gastrointestinal disease, either congenital or acquired, which necessitated parenteral nutrition for a minimum of 24 hours. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of the trials, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The treatment effects were analyzed for each trial, and the results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) and risk differences (RD) for categorical data, and mean differences for continuous data, all with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A fixed-effect model was used for meta-analyses, and sensitivity analyses were performed to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. The review identified three trials involving a total of 274 infants. These trials were methodologically sound but were underpowered to detect clinically significant effects of glutamine supplementation. Meta-analyses did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in the risk of death prior to hospital discharge (typical RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.19 to 3.20; typical RD -0.01, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.03). Similarly, there was no statistically significant difference in the incidence of invasive infections (typical RR 1.37, 95% CI 0.89 to 2.11; typical RD 0.08, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.18). In conclusion, the current evidence from randomized controlled trials does not support the notion that glutamine supplementation provides significant clinical benefits for young infants with severe gastrointestinal disease.
